title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files

reading.body:
This incident shows a general-purpose AI coding and agentic tool being used as operational infrastructure during live cyberattacks. Cursor Agent, which runs on Claude Sonnet, was used by Aurora ransomware operators to conduct hands-on exploitation against target organizations. The tool was not modified or jailbroken in any way the reporting establishes, it was applied to a task, active network intrusion, that falls outside the conditions of legitimate use but within the technical capabilities the product makes available.

The failure mode here is misuse of a deployed agentic AI system rather than a malfunction of that system. The tool performed tasks it was built to perform, writing and executing code, interacting with systems, following operator instructions, but those instructions came from malicious actors. Catching this kind of misuse at deployment time would require behavioral monitoring that distinguishes attack workflows from legitimate development tasks, a boundary that is technically difficult to draw and not established as something Cursor had in place.

What is not established is any finding that Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, was aware of or complicit in this use, or that the attacks against the named organizations succeeded in all cases.

reports.title: Russian-speaking cybercriminals used SpaceX’s Cursor AI tool to hack seven companies
Aurora ransomware targets ESXi, abuses Cursor Agent for exploitation

summary:
Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi environments. The group operates a data leak site and has attacked organizations across multiple countries. Researchers found that Aurora operators used Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation against ten target organizations between April and May 2026. The ESXi ransomware variant encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

The investigation also identified a second Aurora cluster responsible for attacks on eight organizations across Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. This cluster used different methods including SQL Server exploitation, privilege escalation with GodPotato, and data exfiltration to self-hosted storage. Researchers provided indicators of compromise including IP addresses, URLs, and file hashes to help organizations defend against Aurora ransomware attacks.
